content: The preferred approach for treating drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) involves the use of fully oral regimens. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) operational handbook on DR-TB treatment, most patients can be effectively treated with a regimen that begins with four drugs that are either confirmed or likely to be effective. If bedaquiline is discontinued after six months, the regimen will still include three effective agents for the remainder of the treatment. However, if another drug must be stopped due to toxicity, it should be replaced with another effective agent, or bedaquiline may be continued beyond six months under off-label use. When replacing a drug, the replacement should be selected from Group B (unless clofazimine and cycloserine/terizidone are already included) or Group C. The choice of a Group C drug is typically guided by the ranking of the drugs and the specific circumstances of the patient and treatment setting. Recent reviews of observational data have not identified additional safety concerns with the use of bedaquiline beyond six months, but there is no conclusive evidence that prolonged use improves efficacy. Clinicians may consider extending the use of bedaquiline beyond six months and incorporating flexibility in regimen design and the number of effective drugs. To reduce the need for replacing drugs in the regimen, starting with five agents instead of four is an option. This is particularly relevant in cases where reliable drug susceptibility testing (DST) is unavailable for one or more agents, where background resistance to a drug is known to be high, or where a regimen cannot be constructed with at least four effective agents from Groups A and B. Regimen composition may need to be adjusted after treatment initiation as additional clinical or DST information becomes available. If signs of non-response or impending treatment failure emerge, the entire regimen should be reviewed rather than adjusted incrementally. Drugs should be avoided if there is a high likelihood of contraindications, such as kidney or liver dysfunction. When selecting individual drugs for a longer multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) regimen, factors such as resistance patterns, patient comorbidities, and operational considerations (e.g., drug availability and monitoring capacity) must be taken into account. In some cases, hospitalization, surgery, or other adjunctive treatments may be necessary. Comprehensive monitoring and psychosocial support are critical to improving treatment outcomes, and access to palliative and end-of-life care may be required for some patients. Resistance to fluoroquinolones remains a significant concern in all DR-TB regimens. The steps outlined in WHO guidelines for designing regimens for fluoroquinolone-resistant MDR-TB also apply to other resistance patterns. Longer regimens may include more than four drugs, especially when Group C agents are used, to account for uncertainties about the efficacy of some drugs. Specialist advice is essential in such cases to ensure the safest and most effective regimen. The concurrent use of bedaquiline and delamanid, or their use beyond six months, is not currently recommended by WHO due to limited evidence. However, these drugs may be used together in patients with limited treatment options, provided appropriate monitoring (e.g., baseline and follow-up ECG and electrolyte monitoring) is in place. Clinicians may need to make case-by-case decisions in situations where all other options have been exhausted, especially for patients with MDR/RR-TB and fluoroquinolone resistance. Dosages of individual drugs in longer MDR-TB regimens are typically determined by body weight and may need adjustment based on comorbidities or concurrent medications. All TB drugs can generally be started at full doses, but adverse reactions may necessitate temporary or permanent dose modifications. Most agents are administered once daily, although some, like cycloserine and para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), may be given in split doses to reduce adverse effects. Linezolid is usually given once daily, while ethionamide/prothionamide should not be dosed twice daily due to its concentration-dependent killing effect on Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
